CREATORS.summary: Two creator populations ran side by side and neither owned the web outright. Traditional agencies, by now inside four holding companies, still made the ads that carried most of the money — but their pay model was collapsing mid-era. Among large US national advertisers the share paying a media commission fell from 61% in 1994 toward 10% by 2003, and Census data show agency income from commissions and markups sliding from 70% of the industry's take in 1992 to 59% in 1997, with the realized commission rate down to about 11%. Web creative went instead to a new class of interactive shops — Razorfish, Organic, Agency.com, iXL, Scient, USWeb/CKS — that sold strategy and build together, floated on dot-com equity, then died with it: marchFIRST (Whittman-Hart plus USWeb/CKS, formed 1 March 2000) lost $437M in a single quarter and filed Chapter 11 on 13 April 2001. Creative itself was severely constrained: from December 1996 the IAB and CASIE published eight voluntary banner sizes, and the 468x60 full banner under a hard file-size budget became the era's unit of authorship. A third creator class appeared at the very end and had no agency at all: on GoTo/Overture and on Google's AdWords, the advertiser typed its own listing into a web form, and an editorial reviewer, not an art director, decided whether it ran.

BUYERS.summary: The buyer of a web ad in this era was, disproportionately, another internet company spending venture or IPO money. DoubleClick reported that traditional advertisers only passed half of its network revenue in the fourth quarter of 2000 — meaning internet firms had been the majority of demand until then — and Yahoo blamed its 44% marketing-services collapse in 2001 directly on internet companies losing access to capital markets. Across all media the buyer mix barely moved: on the R2b reconciliation national brand money was about 38% of the $247.5B US market in 2000, local retail about 28%, direct response (direct mail, directories, online performance deals and the direct-response money bought inside general media) about 25%, and classified about 9%. Almost none of the local or classified money was online yet: online classifieds were 7% of a $8.2B internet market in 2000, i.e. under 3% of the $21.9B US classified pool. The era's genuinely new buyer class was the self-serve advertiser with no agency: Google signed roughly 350 businesses in AdWords' first month (October 2000), and by December 2001 Overture had about 53,000 paying advertisers, mostly small merchants who had never bought media through an agency at all. That buyer class is era 6's engine; here it is still a rounding error. TAXONOMY SEAM, declared rather than resolved. This era carries TWO money-type splits of the buyer pools. The era-native split above divides directory money by advertiser geography, putting the $11.1B local Yellow Pages block with local retail. The cross-era comparable split, carried beside it as by_money_type_alt, books all $13.2B of directory money as money bought for a counted reply, the rule eras 6 and 7 and the dataset's intent grouping already use; on that rule local-retail buyers spent about $58.9B (23.8 percent) and direct-response buyers about $72.3B (29.2 percent). Cross-era comparisons use the comparable split. Which of the two pools is larger depends on the rule and on nothing else: local retail leads under the geographic rule, direct response leads under the unified rule, and the $11.1B directory block is the sole cause of the flip. No 1994-2001 source records what a Yellow Pages buyer thought it was buying, so no research can settle it. Classified buyers and national-brand buyers are unaffected.

The apparent three-route corroboration is one route wearing three hats, which is why the interval stays wide. || E1 Coen national/local geography residual, WEIGHT 0.60. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the proxy population is 'money bought by a national buyer', the target population is 'money bought on brand terms'; the gap is direct mail, directories, general-media direct response and non-newspaper classified sitting inside the National geography. classified.statement: US classified advertising bought by individuals and small businesses in 2000 was about $21.9B: newspaper classified $19.6B, non-newspaper print classified $1.8-2.3B and online classified $0.5-0.7B. Under 3 percent of the pool had moved online at the top of the boom, and roughly half of the real online classified money sat outside every published advertising series.
classified.method: SOURCED BY: PARTIAL AND DOMINANT. NAA newspaper classified (grade B, all eight years, already in adspend.json as series.naa_newspaper) is $19,608m for 2000 = 89.5 percent of this pool's central, and it is used AS PUBLISHED: a proposed rebasing onto Coen's slightly larger newspaper line (+$153m) is NOT applied, because it is a construction and the source is not. It is corroborated independently at grade A by Knight Ridder's audited FY2000 10-K. THE POOL still grades C, and the reason is precise: the remaining 10.5 percent is unsourced construction, and it is the construction that makes this a pool rather than a newspaper figure. The sourced sub-object is separately recorded at grade B - newspaper classified was 7.923 percent of the observed US total in 2000, with the SHARE peak in 1997 at 8.944 percent (path: 1994 8.145, 1995 8.434, 1996 8.597, 1997 8.944, 1998 8.647, 1999 8.389, 2000 7.923, 2001 7.187), numerator and denominator both published, nothing derived. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 8.63, reference-class 8.85, Fermi-decomposition 9.142) - the tightest agreement in the era, because 89.5 percent of the pool is a real published series. || SOURCE LEG, WEIGHT 0.87: the NAA published series, used as published. || E5 Knight Ridder FY2000 10-K, corroboration only, no weight on the central. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: listed newspaper groups are metro-skewed and metro dailies carry a higher classified share than the small-daily tail of NAA's universe, so the filings figure of 42.5 percent is an UPPER bound on the industry ratio. The 2.2pp gap against NAA's 40.3 percent is in exactly the expected direction and at the expected size. Summing the roughly fifteen public groups' 10-Ks would lift this spine from B to A. || E7 supply-side fringe build, WEIGHT 0.05. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: Coen has never published the composition of its $32,083m miscellaneous bucket, and shoppers and weeklies are demonstrably not inside Coen's newspaper line (Coen $49,050m against NAA $48,670m leaves no room). ADJUSTMENT: bottom-up from roughly 4,000-5,000 free and shopper titles plus 7,000 paid weeklies, capped top-down at half of Coen's $7,665m local miscellaneous, with classified intensity applied separately by publication type (about 45 percent for shoppers, 12-25 percent for paid weeklies, 5-8 percent for trade press) because a shopper IS a classified vehicle while a paid weekly resembles a small daily. || E8 demand-side buyer-count build, WEIGHT 0.05, genuinely independent of E7 and agreeing within 12 percent. || E6 IAB/PwC classifieds share applied to Coen's internet line, WEIGHT 0.03. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: two offsetting definitional biases - IAB's classifieds category absorbs auction listing revenue (overstates) but misses classified sold inside newspaper print-plus-online bundles and, far more importantly, the pure-play job, auto and property portals that sold direct with no agency in the loop (understates). ARITHMETIC DEFECT CORRECTED: the superseded method took 7 percent of IAB's $8,225m total ($576m) against a Coen grand total carrying only $6,507m of internet; on the Coen line the same share is $455m, so the old method imported $121m that was not in the denominator. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses, 2.2pp - the narrowest in the era.

direct_response.statement: US direct-response advertisers' measured media spend in 2000 was about $61.2B, 24.7 percent of the market: direct mail $44.6B, national directories $2.1B, performance-priced internet $0.7-1.4B and direct-response money bought inside general media $5-18.5B. direct_response.method: SOURCED BY: PARTIAL, at component level only. Direct mail $44,591m is Coen's own published line (grade B) and is 73 percent of this pool's central. No source publishes this POOL on this denominator. Two compilers publish incompatible direct-response objects and BOTH are LARGER than the superseded construction: MAGNA's 'Direct' domain (grade A, free for 2000 via Statistical Abstract Table 1279) at $31,108m on a $177.5bn supplier-revenue universe, and DMA/WEFA (grade B) at $191.6bn on a $339.3bn universe that counts $73.2bn of telemarketing. Neither is commensurable with the Coen denominator, so neither wins outright; both constrain the interval and both raise the floor. Grade C. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 22.62, reference-class 24.71, Fermi-decomposition 31.102). The spread is the widest in the era and is driven by two disclosed convention choices, not by conflicting evidence. ROUTE CONSOLIDATION APPLIED BEFORE ANY WEIGHTING. The panel presented about fourteen named routes across three lenses; they collapse to eight independent evidence bases, because routes sharing a common input are one route. The Coen national/local geography residual was offered seven times, MAGNA via Statistical Abstract T1279 six times, the 1997 Economic Census three times, DMA/WEFA three times with three different discount factors, the Knight Ridder 10-K three times, and the IAB format and pricing shares five times. || E1 Coen's own direct mail and Yellow Pages lines, WEIGHT 0.45. Direct mail alone is 18.02pp of the 24.71pp central. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: none for the medium, but a basis gap that is stated rather than adjusted - Coen books direct mail at full advertiser program cost while every other Coen medium is space only. || E2 MAGNA 'Direct' domain, WEIGHT 0.15. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: MAGNA's direct mail is carriage-only supplier revenue at $18,250m against Coen's $44,591m full advertiser outlay, a documented 2.44x. ADJUSTMENT: substitute Coen's direct-mail line into MAGNA's own classification and gross the denominator by the same amount, giving $57,449m / $203,841m = 28.2 percent - and MAGNA's Direct excludes direct-response TV, print and radio and telemarketing by its own construction, so 28.2 percent is a FLOOR from an independent compiler's own structure. Two lenses derived this separately. || E4 DMA/WEFA direct-marketing-by-medium, WEIGHT 0.20, CEILING-SETTING. PROXY-POPULATION GAP, and it is large: DMA measures response-CARRYING placements and includes traffic generation (drive-to-store with a call to action), not response-BOUGHT money; it counts telemarketing as advertising; its newspaper direct-response share of 37.3 percent ($18.4bn) almost exactly reproduces NAA's classified ($19.6bn), so it double-counts against the classified pool; and its direct-mail line matches Coen to $9m, proving it is NOT independent on the very medium it appears to corroborate. ADJUSTMENT: applied raw it yields $104.2bn of general-media direct response and a 48.9 percent pool, which all three lenses reject; the discounts applied ranged from a 3x medium-by-medium discount (to $18.5bn) through a roughly 75 percent discount (to $7.9bn) to a bottom-up rebuild (about $5.0bn). || E10 and E11, the ERA/infomercial direct-response-TV build and the PIB 1993 magazine mail-order category, WEIGHT 0.15 combined. These are the ONLY genuinely independent checks on the general-media direct-response quantity, and both land at the bottom of the range: ERA's $11bn of US direct-TV sales less $8.5bn of shopping-channel owned airtime that is outside measured advertising implies $3.5-5.3bn of direct-response television against DMA's $21.9bn, and PIB's magazine mail-order category was 9.8 percent of Coen magazines in 1993 against DMA's 56.6 percent. || E6 IAB/PwC pricing-model split, WEIGHT 0.05. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: IAB's denominator ($8,087-8,225m) exceeds Coen's internet line ($6,507m), so the share must be applied to Coen's line or money absent from the denominator is imported. ARITHMETIC DEFECT CORRECTED: the superseded method took 10 percent of IAB's $8,225m ($822m) against a denominator carrying $6,507m of internet; on the Coen line it is $651m, so the old method imported $172m. || E9 USPS Standard Mail (A) postage revenue, WEIGHT 0.0 on the central but named because it ADJUDICATES the basis: at roughly $15-16bn in FY2000 it puts Coen at 2.8-3.0x postage (postage plus production, creative and list rental, i.e. total advertiser outlay) and MAGNA at 1.15x (media-owner revenue plus a thin margin). Since a money-type split asks where ADVERTISER money goes, Coen's basis is the correct one for this partition. This route narrows the interval rather than widening it. || STATEMENT DEFECT CORRECTED: the superseded method said direct-response television and print insertions 'are not separable in the Coen series'. Not separable in COEN is true; not separable is false - DMA/WEFA published them by medium for 2000 (DR-television $21.9bn, DR-newspaper $18.4bn, DR-magazine $9.8bn, DR-radio $7.7bn). They need heavy discounting but they are not zero. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses, 17.0pp - the widest in the era, and correctly so.

local_retail.statement: On the cross-era comparable rule, where ALL directory money sits in the same intent pool eras 6 and 7 use, US local-retail advertisers' measured media spend in 2000 was about $58.9B, 23.8 percent of the market. That is the era-native pool (e5-buyers-011, $70.1B) less the local Yellow Pages block, $11.1B, which this rule books as money bought for a counted reply rather than as local money. Under the era-native geographic rule local retail leads direct response, 28.32 to 24.71; under this unified-intent rule direct response leads local retail, 29.21 to 23.82. The flip is exact and this one block is its sole cause. Under BOTH rules the two intervals still overlap, so the pair stays unranked by interval and a chart must not sort these two bars. No 1994-2001 evidence decides which rule is right; both are carried.
local_retail.method: TAXONOMY: unified-intent. This is the CROSS-ERA COMPARABLE view of era 5's local-retail pool, and it is a declared definitional seam, not a correction. The era-native claim (e5-scale-011 / e5-buyers-011) stands unchanged at 28.32 percent and is the view era 5 reports on its own terms. || THE BLOCK THAT MOVES: local Yellow Pages, $11,135m in 2000, which is 4.4995 percent of the observed $247,472m Coen total. The national directory leg, $2,093m, already sits in direct response under both rules, so only the local leg moves. Both legs are Coen's own published Yellow Pages line for 2000 ($13,228m) split by advertiser geography. || DERIVATION: this claim inherits the era-native pool's whole evidence base, three-lens panel and aggregation rule, and changes exactly one convention. Central = 28.32 - 4.4995 = 23.82 percent, $70,084m - $11,135m = $58,949m. Every other input is untouched: the Coen Total Local residual (E1, weight 0.60), the 1997 Economic Census local receipts check (E3, weight 0.15), the supply-side and demand-side shopper-and-weekly classified fringe builds (E7/E8, weight 0.10 combined, independent of each other and agreeing within 12 percent), the DMA/WEFA local share of general-media direct response (E4, weight 0.05) and MAGNA Local as a ceiling only (E2, weight 0.10, interval only). The containment check still holds and was not re-run because it does not touch directories: NAA retail $21,409m + NAA classified $19,608m = $41,017m sits inside Coen's local newspaper line of $41,821m with $804m to spare, verified for all eight years. || INTERVAL, and it NARROWS rather than shifting whole. Native ci80 [20.8, 33.0], 12.2pp wide. UPPER BOUND: 33.0 - 4.4995 = 28.50. The native ceiling was set by the reference-class and Fermi lenses, both of which carried the local directory block inside this pool, so removing the block lowers the ceiling by the whole block. LOWER BOUND: unchanged at 20.8. SELLERS.summary: Web inventory concentrated faster than any earlier medium. The ten largest online ad sellers took 71% of US internet ad revenue in the fourth quarter of 2000 and 77% a year later; the top 25 took 91% and the top 50 took 98%. Those sellers were portals — search engines and portals alone accounted for 36% of revenue by content genre in 2000 — and their business was a magazine business with a server: Yahoo booked $1,110M of net revenue in 2000, of which $968M was banners and sponsorships, at an 86.5% gross margin. Between the portal and the advertiser sat a second layer that took a real cut: DoubleClick's network arm ran a 25-40% gross margin, meaning publishers kept roughly 60-75% of network-sold money, while its ad-serving arm charged separately and served 621 billion ads worldwide in 2000. In paid search the intermediary cut was far larger and pointed the other way: Overture paid out 56% of 2001 revenue as traffic acquisition cost to the portals and browsers that sent it queries, because more than 95% of its traffic came from affiliates. The shakeout was brutal and fast — Excite@Home filed Chapter 11 on 1 October 2001, and Yahoo's revenue fell 35% in a single year.

MEDIUM.summary: The era's headline is not that the web arrived but that it barely dented the ranking. Newspapers were the largest single US medium every year from 1994 through 2000, peaking at $49.05B; direct mail then overtook them in 2001 ($44.7B against $44.3B) and stayed ahead. Yellow Pages, the structural ancestor of paid search, grew right through the web's arrival, from $9.8B in 1994 to $13.2B in 2000. Newspaper classified peaked at $19.6B in 2000, about 40% of newspaper advertising revenue, with recruitment alone at $8.7B. Against those, the internet reached somewhere between 2.6% and 3.7% of US ad spend in 2000 depending on whose internet number and whose denominator you use, then shrank in 2001. Two definitional cautions matter inside this window: the Coen series has no internet line at all before 1997, so 1994-1996 web spend is reconstruction, not data; and 'Out of Home' replaced 'Billboards' as a Coen category in 2000 at roughly three times the expenditure ($4.78B against $1.73B on the 1999 overlap), an artefact that will look like a real jump on any chart that does not annotate it.

SCALE.summary: US measured advertising grew from $153.0B in 1994 to $247.5B in 2000, the largest run in the series' post-war history, then fell 6.5% to $231.3B in 2001 — one of only six down years in seventy (the others being 1938, 1942, 1961 and 1991). Advertising's share of GDP peaked in 2000 at roughly 2.3-2.5% depending on the series and the GDP vintage, and has never regained that level, which makes 2000 the high-water mark of advertising intensity in the American economy and complicates any story in which the web enlarged the pie. Internet advertising itself went from unmeasurable in 1994-1995 to $267M in 1996, $8.1-8.2B in 2000 and back to $7.1-7.2B in 2001, with four consecutive quarterly declines from the Q4 2000 peak of $2.16B. By money type in 2000, on the R2b three-lens reconciliation, the market split roughly $94.9B national brand, $70.1B local retail, $61.2B direct response and $21.9B classified — and the two pools search would later take, classified and direct response, were together worth $83.1B while the entire internet ad market was worth $8.2B. Newspaper classified's SHARE of US advertising peaked in 1997 at 8.94 percent, three years before its dollar peak. TAXONOMY SEAM, declared rather than resolved. This era carries TWO money-type splits, and the difference is worth $13.2B in 2000, 5.35 points of that year's market. The era-native split above divides directory money by advertiser geography: local Yellow Pages ($11,135m) counts as local money, national directories ($2,093m) as response money. The cross-era comparable split, carried beside it as by_money_type_alt, puts ALL directory money in the response pool, which is the rule era 6, era 7, the dataset's own intent grouping and MAGNA all use; on that rule local retail is 23.82 percent ($58.9B) and direct response is 29.21 percent ($72.3B). Any comparison that crosses eras must use the comparable split. The rank of local retail against direct response depends entirely on which rule is chosen: local retail leads on the geographic rule, 28.32 to 24.71, and direct response leads on the unified rule, 29.21 to 23.82. No evidence from 1994-2001 adjudicates the choice, so this is an editorial rule and not a finding. National brand and classified are identical under both rules.

claims.method: The four pool medians sum to 100.22 percent of the observed 2000 total, over-allocating the $247,472m observed total by $544m. This is not a measurement gap and not a shortfall: it is an exact, fully attributable artefact of the median operator. Each of the three lenses individually reconciles to 100.000 percent by construction, but the median of a partition is not itself a partition. The over-allocation traces to a single swap: the medians for national brand (38.34), local retail (28.32) and direct response (24.71) all come from the Fermi-decomposition lens, whose own four values sum to 100.00 with classified at 8.63; the classified median is 8.85, from the reference-class lens, and 8.85 - 8.63 = 0.22 exactly. BOUNDS: taking the mean of lens centrals instead of the median reconciles to 100.000 exactly, and dropping any one lens and taking the mean of the remaining two also reconciles to within 0.003pp, so the residual cannot exceed roughly half a point under any plausible re-specification of the aggregation rule. It is left standing rather than smoothed away, because scaling the four pools by 0.9978 would silently move each headline off the plain median the rigor standard requires. || SECOND, LARGER RESIDUAL, WHICH NO FORCING CAN ABSORB. The in-universe residual above is trivial, but the observed Coen universe excludes money that functionally belongs in these pools. (a) TELEMARKETING: DMA counts $73.2bn of it as advertising in 2000; Coen counts none. That is 29.6 percent of the observed total, and if it were in the denominator direct response would dominate every other pool. PRICING.summary: The web's founding pricing decision was to copy the magazine. HotWired priced its October 1994 launch sponsorships at $30,000 for twelve weeks because a page in Wired cost about $10,000 a month, and the industry then generalised that into the CPM: 43% of US internet ad revenue was priced purely per thousand impressions in 2000, and another 47% on hybrid deals that started from a CPM. Rate cards behaved like magazine rate cards too — around $37 CPM for an average banner in December 1997, still $25 for a full banner in Q4 2000 — but realised prices did not, because unsold inventory diluted everything. Portal 'anchor tenancy' deals rebuilt the sponsorship logic of 1930s radio: Excite paid Netscape $5.0M for each of two Premier Provider slots in 1996 and a minimum $8.25M in 1997. Against all of this, GoTo.com from June 1998 sold a completely different thing: not an impression but a click, ranked purely by bid, paid at the bid, minimum five cents, with the advertiser setting the price. Overture's average realised price per click was $0.23 in Q4 2001. Google's answer in October 2000 was still a CPM — AdWords launched with fixed $15, $12 and $10 CPM tiers — which is exactly why era 6 begins where it does.

MEASUREMENT.summary: This is the first era in which the seller counted the audience with its own instrument and the buyer had no third-party audit to appeal to. The counting technology was the ad server: DoubleClick's DART delivered 621 billion ads worldwide in 2000 and its log was the invoice. Two rival counting institutions grew up beside it — server-side log auditors (I/PRO, NetCount, ABC Interactive) and user-panel meters (Media Metrix, RelevantKnowledge, then Nielsen//NetRatings from 1998) — and they disagreed, because proxy caching hid impressions from server logs while panels missed work and school access. Standard-setting was industry-funded and voluntary: the IAB and CASIE published eight banner sizes on 10 December 1996, and Procter & Gamble convened about 200 industry leaders at the FAST summit in Cincinnati in August 1998 precisely because only 16% of marketers said they were satisfied with online ad measurement. The number the whole market watched, the click-through rate, fell from double digits at HotWired's launch to roughly 0.3% by 2000 — a fall in the very metric that had justified the medium's premium CPMs, and the reason a pay-per-click seller could credibly attack the impression.

TARGETING.summary: Targeting in this era ran on two incompatible logics, and the losing one was the more advanced. The dominant logic was profile-based: DoubleClick's DART used cookies to target by site, domain, geography, browser, time of day and frequency cap across a network reaching 48% of the US internet audience, and in 1999 DoubleClick bought Abacus, whose direct-mail cooperative database covered purchase histories on roughly 90% of US households. Merging the two would have given the web named-person targeting; EPIC's FTC complaint of 10 February 2000 and the resulting investigation forced DoubleClick to abandon the plan on 2 March 2000, and the first great privacy retreat of the ad-tech era happened before third-party behavioural targeting ever really shipped. The other logic was intent: GoTo/Overture matched the advertisement to the words the user had just typed, which needed no profile at all and no cookie. It was tiny — keyword search was 1% of US internet ad revenue in 2000 — but it delivered 442 million clicks in Q4 2001 alone, and Overture's own filing sized the opportunity against Yellow Pages calls and direct-mail responses rather than against banner impressions.

open_defect.where: The secondary share in this claim's statement, and the identical phrase in the parent event's desc field.
open_defect.problem: 'close to 20% of the 61 spots available' cannot be true against the counts stated in the same sentence. 21/61 = 34.4 percent; the narrower count 14/61 = 23.0 percent; and 20 percent of 61 = 12.2 ads, which matches neither 14 nor 21. Everything else in the sentence reconciles: 14 + 5 + 2 = 21, and $44M / 21 = $2.10M per spot against the stated ~$2.2M.

Two readings are open - a corrupted 'close to 20 OF the 61 spots' (21 is close to 20), or the true share of about a third - and 34 percent and 20 percent tell materially different stories about how far the bubble reached into the Super Bowl. Writing either without re-reading the Wikipedia and Fast Company sources would be inventing a replacement number, which this repair does not do.

open_defect.chapter_exposure: None. Chapter 06 (06-the-impression.md) carries only the fourteen in-game advertisers and the ~$2.2M spot price, neither of which is affected.
open_defect.source_carries_the_error: The figure is NOT a paraphrase error introduced by this project: the R3 verdict on this claim quotes the cited Wikipedia article as saying the 21 ads 'amounted to nearly 20% of the 61 spots available', and R3 imported that string verbatim. The impossibility therefore sits in the source, so repairing it means deciding whether to correct the source's arithmetic (about a third), read it as a corrupted 'nearly 20 OF the 61 spots', or drop the share entirely. That is a human call on the source, not a data-entry fix.

events.title: Excite@Home files for Chapter 11 as the portal model breaks
events.desc: Excite@Home, formed by a $6.7 billion merger and once worth about $35 billion, filed for Chapter 11 on 1 October 2001 and agreed to sell its network to AT&T for $307 million. In the same month GoTo.com renamed itself Overture Services. The two events together are the era's hinge: the impression-selling portal failed while the click-selling auction survived and grew through the same downturn.

events.title: The crash resets the market
events.desc: US internet advertising revenue fell about 12% for the year to $7.1-7.2 billion after four consecutive quarterly declines, and total US measured advertising fell 6.5% to $231.3 billion — one of only six down years in seventy. Banners fell from 48% to 36% of internet revenue, barter rose from 6% to 10%, seller concentration rose to 77% for the top ten, and performance-priced deals rose from 10% to 12%. Impression pricing survived the crash smaller; performance pricing came out of it larger.

IAB press release, 'Internet Advertising Revenue Totaled $1.7 Billion for Q4 2001'

revenue_per_unit.statement: Effective revenue per delivered US web ad impression in 2000, the era's peak year — about $7 per thousand, against rate cards of $25-$35 per thousand for a full banner. The gap is unsold inventory, volume discounting, house ads and barter, exactly as DoubleClick described it: 'increases in the amounts of unsold inventory, which diluted the effective price of delivered advertising impressions.'
revenue_per_unit.method: Numerator: impression-priced US internet ad revenue in 2000 = banners (48%) plus sponsorships (28%) of IAB/PwC FY2000 revenue $8.225B = $6.25B. Denominator: US delivered display impressions in 2000, triangulated three ways. (1) AdRelevance measured 172 billion US impressions in Q4 2000 and 65 billion in December 2000; with Q4 the seasonal peak at roughly 28-30% of the year, that implies 575-615 billion for 2000, and AdRelevance's monitoring method undercounts unmeasured sites, so treat it as a floor. (2) DoubleClick's DART served 621 billion ads worldwide in 2000 for 2,000+ clients; DART was the largest but far from the only ad server (Yahoo, AOL and MSN ran their own; AdForce, Engage and 24/7 competed), so if DART was 25-40% of worldwide served ads the worldwide total was 1.6-2.5 trillion and the US share roughly half of that. (3) Yahoo alone delivered about 784 million page views per day ex-Japan in December 2000, roughly 24 billion in the month. Taking the three together, US delivered display impressions in 2000 were between 0.6 and 1.5 trillion, central 0.9 trillion. $6.25B / 0.9T = $0.0069 per impression. boundary_notes:
Shared with era 4 (1976-1993, Segmentation): the Coen/McCann series total for 1993 is $140.956B, rising to $153.024B in 1994, so era 4 should close on 1993 and era 5 open on 1994 with no gap. Direct mail was $27.266B in 1993 and Yellow Pages $9.517B; both grew through the whole of era 5. Newspapers were the largest single US medium at the end of era 4 ($32.025B in 1993) and remained so until 2000, so neither era should claim a medium crossover at the 1993/94 boundary. Agency compensation: 61% of large national advertisers still paid commissions in 1994, so era 4 owns the start of the commission's decline (71% in 1982) and era 5 owns its middle.

Shared with era 6 (2002-2008, The Auction): era 5 ends with the mechanism in place but not yet dominant. As of December 2001 Overture ran a pure first-price, pure-bid auction with a $0.05 minimum bid, human editorial review, ~53,000 advertisers, 442 million paid introductions in the quarter, an average realised price of $0.23 per click, and traffic acquisition costs of 56% of revenue. Overture's FY2001 revenue was $288.133M; Google's total FY2001 revenue was $86.4M. Era 6 therefore inherits Overture as the paid-search revenue leader, consistent with the pre-cleared constraint that Overture led through 2002 ($667.7M FY2002). AdWords existed from 23 October 2000 as a fixed-CPM self-serve product at $15/$12/$10 per thousand impressions; the auction (AdWords Select) is a February 2002 event and belongs to era 6, as does the AOL syndication flip of May 2002, the April 2004 trademark-keyword policy change, and the 2004 Overture patent settlement (~2.7M shares, ~$230M). Era 6 also inherits the pools search will take: US classified peaked at $19.6B in 2000 (about 40% of newspaper ad revenue, recruitment $8.7B) and Yellow Pages was $13.228B in 2000 and still rising, while total US internet advertising was only $7.1-8.2B. The internet ad market handed to era 6 is $7.1-7.2B for 2001 (IAB/PwC), 48% CPM-priced, 40% hybrid, 12% performance, with the top ten sellers holding 77%. Total US measured ad spend handed over is $231.287B for 2001 (Coen), having peaked at $247.472B in 2000 at roughly 2.4% of GDP — a peak share never regained, which means era 6's growth story must be told as reallocation, not expansion.

Series and definition warnings that both neighbours must carry: (1) the Coen series has no internet line before 1997, so 1994-1996 web spend is reconstruction; (2) 'Out of Home' replaced 'Billboards' as a Coen category in 2000 at roughly 2.8x the expenditure on the 1999 overlap year; (3) Coen is bottom-up advertiser billings at list prices while IAB/PwC is top-down seller revenue, which is why Coen's internet line ($6.507B in 2000) sits about 20% below IAB's ($8.087-8.225B) and the two must never be mixed inside one line.
